title: IX. The Devil. Ivan’s Nightmare
paragraphs: I'm not a doctor, but even so I feel the moment has come when I have to give the reader some account of the nature of Ivan's illness. Getting ahead of events, I can say at least this much: he was, at that very moment, on the verge of an attack of brain fever. His health had been affected for some time, but had put up a stubborn resistance to the fever, which in the end gained complete mastery over it. Knowing nothing of medicine, I'll venture the suggestion that he had, in fact, perhaps through a terrible effort of will, managed to delay the attack for a while, hoping, of course, to stop it entirely. He knew he wasn't well, but he loathed the thought of being ill at this fatal moment, at the approaching crisis of his life, when he needed his wits fully about him, to say what he had to say boldly and firmly, and "to justify himself to himself."

He had, however, gone to consult the new doctor, brought from Moscow by one of Katerina Ivanovna's fanciful notions, which I've already mentioned. After listening to him and examining him, the doctor concluded that he really was suffering from some disorder of the brain, and wasn't at all surprised by the admission Ivan reluctantly made him. "Hallucinations are quite likely, given your condition," the doctor said, "though it would be best to verify them.... You need to take steps right away, without a moment's delay, or things will go badly for you." But Ivan didn't follow this sound advice and didn't take to his bed to be nursed. "I'm still walking around, so I'm strong enough—if I collapse, that'll be a different matter, and anyone who wants to can nurse me then," he decided, dropping the subject.

And so he sat there, half-aware himself that he was delirious, and, as I've already said, staring persistently at something on the sofa against the opposite wall. Someone seemed to be sitting there, though goodness knows how he'd gotten in, since he hadn't been in the room when Ivan came in, on his return from Smerdyakov's. This was a person—or, more precisely, a Russian gentleman of a particular type, no longer young, qui faisait la cinquantaine, as the French say, with rather long, still-thick dark hair, faintly streaked with gray, and a small pointed beard. He wore a brownish reefer jacket, somewhat shabby, evidently cut by a good tailor, though at least three years out of fashion—a style that smart, well-off people had abandoned two years before. His linen and his long, scarf-like necktie were of the kind worn by people aiming at style, but on closer look his linen wasn't especially clean, and his wide scarf was quite threadbare. The visitor's checked trousers were excellently cut, but too pale in color and too tight for current fashion. His soft, fluffy white hat was out of step with the season.

In short, he presented every appearance of gentility on limited means. It looked as though the gentleman belonged to that class of idle landowners who once flourished in the days of serfdom. He'd unmistakably moved, at some point, in good, fashionable society, had once had solid connections, quite possibly still kept some of them—but after a lively youth, growing gradually poorer once serfdom was abolished, he'd sunk into the position of a poor relation of the better sort, drifting from one old family friend to another, welcomed for his agreeable, accommodating manner, and as, after all, a gentleman who could be seated with anyone, though of course not in a place of honor. Gentlemen of this accommodating temperament and dependent standing, who can tell a good story, take a hand at cards, and have a distinct aversion to any duty forced upon them, are usually solitary creatures, either bachelors or widowers. Sometimes they have children, but if so, the children are always being raised somewhere far off, at some aunt's, whom these gentlemen never mention in good company, seeming ashamed of the connection. They gradually lose track of their children altogether, though now and then they receive a birthday or Christmas letter, and sometimes even answer it.

The unexpected visitor's face wasn't so much good-natured as accommodating, ready to take on any agreeable expression the moment called for. He had no watch, but carried a tortoiseshell lorgnette on a black ribbon. On the middle finger of his right hand sat a heavy gold ring set with a cheap opal.

Ivan sat silent, angry, unwilling to start the conversation. The visitor waited, sitting exactly like a poor relation who'd come down from his room to keep his host company at tea, discreetly quiet, seeing that his host was frowning and preoccupied. But he was ready for any friendly conversation the moment his host began it. All at once his face took on a look of sudden concern.

"I say," he began, to Ivan, "forgive me, I only mention it as a reminder. You went to Smerdyakov's to find out about Katerina Ivanovna, but you came away without learning a thing about her—you must have forgotten—"

"Ah, yes," broke from Ivan, his face darkening with unease. "Yes, I'd forgotten... but never mind now, it doesn't matter, till tomorrow," he muttered to himself, "and you," he added, turning to his visitor, "I would have remembered that myself in another minute, since that was exactly what was tormenting me! Why do you butt in, as if I'm supposed to believe you put it in my head, and that I didn't remember it on my own?"

"Then don't believe it," the gentleman said, smiling amiably. "What good is believing against your will, anyway? Besides, proof doesn't help belief along, especially material proof. Thomas believed not because he saw the risen Christ, but because he wanted to believe, before he ever saw. Take the spiritualists, for instance.... I'm quite fond of them... just imagine, they think they're serving the cause of religion, because devils show them their horns from the other world. That, they say, is a material proof, so to speak, of the existence of another world. The other world and material proof—what next! And if it comes to that, does proving there's a devil prove there's a God? I'd like to join an idealist society—I'd lead the opposition in it, I'd say I'm a realist, not a materialist, heh heh!"

"Listen," Ivan suddenly got up from the table. "I seem to be delirious.... I am delirious, in fact—say whatever nonsense you like, I don't care! You won't drive me into a fury the way you did last time. But somehow I feel ashamed.... I want to walk around the room.... Sometimes I don't see you and don't even hear your voice the way I did last time, but I can always guess what you're babbling on about, because it's me, it's me myself talking, not you. Only I don't know whether I was dreaming last time or really saw you. I'll wet a towel and put it on my head, and maybe you'll dissolve into thin air."
Ivan went to the corner, got a towel, and did as he'd said, and with a wet towel on his head began pacing up and down the room.
"I'm so glad you're being so familiar with me," the visitor began.

"Fool," Ivan laughed. "Do you think I'm going to stand on ceremony with you? I'm in good spirits right now, even with this pain in my forehead... and at the crown of my head... only please don't talk philosophy, the way you did last time. If you can't take yourself off, talk about something amusing. Gossip—you're a poor relation, you ought to gossip. What a nightmare to have! But I'm not afraid of you. I'll get the better of you. I won't be carted off to a madhouse!"

"C'est charmant, poor relation. Yes, that's exactly my true shape. What else am I on earth but a poor relation? By the way, I'm listening to you, and I'm rather surprised to find you're actually starting to take me for something real, and not simply your own fancy, as you kept insisting last time—"

"Not for one minute have I taken you for reality," Ivan cried, in a kind of fury. "You're a lie, you're my illness, you're a phantom. It's only that I don't know how to destroy you, and I see I'll have to suffer through it for a while. You're my hallucination. You're the embodiment of myself—but only one side of me... of my thoughts and feelings, and only the nastiest and stupidest ones at that. From that angle you might interest me, if only I had time to waste on you—"

"Excuse me, excuse me, I've caught you now. When you flew at Alyosha under the streetlamp tonight and shouted at him, 'You learned it from him! How do you know he visits me?'—you were thinking of me right then. So for one brief moment, you did believe that I really exist," the gentleman laughed, blandly.
"Yes, that was a moment of weakness... but I couldn't believe in you. I don't know whether I was asleep or awake last time. Maybe I was only dreaming, then, and never really saw you at all—"
"And why were you so surly with Alyosha just now? He's a dear boy; I did him wrong over Father Zossima."
"Don't talk about Alyosha! How dare you, you lackey!" Ivan laughed again.
"You scold me, but you laugh—that's a good sign. But you're ever so much more polite than you were last time, and I know why: that great resolution of yours—"
"Don't speak of my resolution," Ivan cried, savagely.
"I understand, I understand, c'est noble, c'est charmant—you're going to defend your brother and sacrifice yourself... C'est chevaleresque."
"Hold your tongue, or I'll kick you!"

"I wouldn't mind that at all, since it would achieve my object. If you kick me, you'll have to believe I'm real, since people don't kick ghosts. Joking aside, it makes no difference to me—scold away if you like, though you might be a bit more polite even to me. 'Fool, lackey!' Such words!"
"Scolding you, I scold myself," Ivan laughed again. "You are myself, myself, just with a different face. You only say what I'm already thinking... you're incapable of saying anything new!"
"If I think the way you do, that's entirely to my credit," the gentleman said, with delicacy and dignity.

"You only pick out my worst thoughts—and what's more, the stupid ones. You're stupid and vulgar. You're horribly stupid. No, I can't stand you! What am I supposed to do, what am I supposed to do?" Ivan said, through clenched teeth.

"My dear friend, above everything else I want to behave like a gentleman, and to be recognized as one," the visitor began, with a kind of deprecating, simple-hearted pride typical of a poor relation. "I'm poor, but... I won't say very honest, but... it's a generally accepted axiom in society that I'm a fallen angel. I really can't conceive how I could ever have been an angel. If I ever was, it must have been so long ago there's no harm in forgetting it now. These days I only value the reputation of being a gentlemanly sort, and I live as best I can, trying to make myself agreeable. I genuinely love mankind, I've been terribly slandered! Here, staying with you from time to time, my life takes on a kind of reality, and that's what I like best of all. You see, like you, I suffer from the fantastical, and so I love the realism of earth. Here, with you, everything's bounded, everything's formulated and geometrical, while over there we've got nothing but indeterminate equations! I wander around here dreaming. I like dreaming. Besides, on earth I turn superstitious. Please don't laugh, that's exactly what I like—turning superstitious. I take on all your habits here: I've grown fond of going to the public baths, would you believe it, and I go steam myself with merchants and priests. What I dream of is becoming incarnate once and for all, irrevocably, in the shape of some merchant's wife weighing eighteen stone, and believing everything she believes. My ideal is to go to church and light a candle in simple, wholehearted faith—upon my word, it is. Then all my suffering would end. I like being treated for illness, too. This spring there was an outbreak of smallpox, and I went and got vaccinated at a foundling hospital—if only you knew how much I enjoyed that day. I subscribed ten roubles to the Slavic cause!... But you're not listening. Do you know, you're not at all well tonight? I know you went to see that doctor yesterday... well, how's your health? What did the doctor say?"
"Fool!" Ivan snapped.
"But you're clever, all the same. Scolding again? I wasn't asking out of sympathy. You don't need to answer. Now the rheumatism's come back again—"
"Fool!" Ivan repeated.
"You keep saying the same thing; but I had such an attack of rheumatism last year that I remember it to this very day."
"The devil, with rheumatism!"
"Why not, if I sometimes take on fleshly form? I put on flesh, and I take the consequences. Satan sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto."
"What, what—Satan sum et nihil humanum... not bad, for the devil!"
"I'm glad I've finally pleased you."
"But you didn't get that from me." Ivan stopped suddenly, struck. "That never crossed my mind—that's strange."

"C'est du nouveau, n'est-ce pas? This time I'll be honest and explain it to you. Listen: in dreams, and especially in nightmares—from indigestion, or anything else—a man sometimes sees such artistic visions, such intricate, real actuality, such events, even a whole world of events woven into such a plot, with such unexpected details, from the most exalted matters down to the last button on a cuff, that I swear Leo Tolstoy himself has never invented the like. And yet such dreams are sometimes had not by writers, but by the most ordinary people—officials, journalists, priests.... The whole subject is a complete mystery. A certain statesman once confessed to me, in fact, that all his best ideas came to him while he was asleep. Well, that's how it is right now—though I'm your hallucination, still, just as in a nightmare, I'm saying original things that hadn't occurred to you before. So I'm not repeating your ideas, and yet I'm only your nightmare, nothing more."
"You're lying. Your whole aim is to convince me you exist separately, and aren't my nightmare, and now you're claiming you're a dream."
"My dear fellow, I've adopted a special method today—I'll explain it to you afterward. Wait, where did I leave off? Oh, yes! I caught cold that time, only not here, but over there."

"Where's over there? Tell me, will you be here long? Can't you go away?" Ivan exclaimed, almost in despair. He stopped pacing, sat down on the sofa, leaned his elbows on the table again, and gripped his head tight in both hands. He yanked off the wet towel and flung it away in irritation. It was clearly no use.

"Your nerves are out of order," the gentleman observed, in an easy, careless, though perfectly polite tone. "You're even angry at me for having caught cold, though it happened in the most natural way. I was rushing off at the time to a diplomatic soirée at the house of a high-ranking lady in Petersburg, one aiming at some influence at the Ministry. Well—evening dress, white tie, gloves—though I was God knows where, and had to fly across space to reach your earth.... Of course it took only an instant, but you know a ray of light from the sun takes a full eight minutes, and imagine, in evening dress and an open waistcoat. Spirits don't freeze, but once you're in fleshly form, well... in short, I didn't think it through, and set off, and you know, out in that ethereal space, in the water above the firmament, there's such a frost... at least, one can hardly call it frost, imagine, a hundred and fifty degrees below zero! You know that game the village girls play—inviting the unwary to lick an axe in thirty degrees of frost, and the tongue freezes to it instantly, and the poor fool tears the skin off, and it bleeds. But that's only at thirty degrees; at a hundred and fifty, I'd imagine just touching your finger to the axe would finish you off... if only there were an axe out there."
"And could there be an axe out there?" Ivan cut in, offhand and disdainful. He was straining with everything he had not to believe in the delusion, not to sink into outright madness.
"An axe?" the guest broke in, surprised.
"Yes—what would happen to an axe out there?" Ivan suddenly cried, with a sort of wild, insistent stubbornness.

"What would become of an axe in space? Quelle idée! If it happened to fall some distance, I imagine it would start flying around the earth without knowing why, like a satellite. Astronomers would calculate the rising and setting of the axe, Gatzuk would put it in his almanac, that's all there is to it."

"You're stupid, horribly stupid," Ivan said, peevishly. "Lie more cleverly, or I won't listen. You want to win me over with realism, to convince me you're real—but I don't want to believe you're real! I won't believe it!"

"But I'm not lying, it's all the truth; the trouble is, the truth is hardly ever amusing. I can see you keep expecting something grand from me, and maybe something fine. That's a great shame, because I can only give what I have—"
"Don't talk philosophy, you jackass!"

"Philosophy, indeed, when my whole right side is numb and I'm moaning and groaning. I've tried the entire medical profession: they diagnose beautifully, they've got the whole of your illness at their fingertips, but they haven't the first idea how to cure it. There was an eager young student here—'You may die,' he told me, 'but you'll know perfectly well what disease you're dying of!' And then there's their way of shunting people off to specialists! 'We only diagnose,' they say, 'go to such-and-such a specialist, he'll cure you.' The old-fashioned doctor who used to cure everything has completely vanished, I promise you—now it's nothing but specialists, and they all advertise in the papers. If something's wrong with your nose, they send you to Paris—there, they say, is a European specialist who cures noses. You go to Paris, he examines your nose; 'I can only treat your right nostril,' he'll tell you, 'I don't treat the left, that's not my specialty—but go to Vienna, there's a specialist there who'll fix your left nostril.' What's a man to do? I turned to folk remedies. A German doctor advised me to rub myself with honey and salt at the bathhouse. Purely to get an extra bath out of it, I went, smeared myself all over, and it did nothing for me at all. In despair I wrote to Count Mattei in Milan. He sent me a book and some drops, bless him, and just imagine—Hoff's malt extract cured me! I bought it by accident, drank a bottle and a half, and I was ready to dance—it cleared it right up. I decided to write to the papers to thank him, out of pure gratitude, and just imagine, it caused no end of trouble: not a single paper would print my letter. 'It would look far too reactionary,' they said, 'no one will believe it. Le diable n'existe point. You'd better stay anonymous,' they advised me. What good is a thank-you letter if it's anonymous? I laughed it over with the men at the newspaper office. 'It's reactionary to believe in God nowadays,' I said, 'but I'm the devil, so people are allowed to believe in me.' 'We quite understand that,' they said. 'Who doesn't believe in the devil? Still, it won't do, it might damage our reputation. As a joke, if you like.' But I figured as a joke it wouldn't be terribly witty. So it never got printed. And you know, it still stings me to this day. My best feelings—gratitude, for instance—are literally denied me, simply because of my social standing."
"Philosophical reflections again?" Ivan snarled, viciously.

"God forbid, but a man can't help complaining sometimes. I'm a slandered creature. You reproach me every other minute for being stupid. One can tell you're young. My dear fellow, intelligence isn't the only thing! I have, by nature, a kind and cheerful heart. 'I also write vaudevilles of every sort.' You seem to take me for an aged Hlestakov, but my fate is a far more serious one. Before time itself began, by some decree I've never been able to work out, I was predestined 'to deny'—and yet I'm genuinely good-hearted and not the least bit inclined toward negation. 'No, you must go and deny, because without denial there's no criticism, and what would a journal be without a criticism column?' Without criticism there'd be nothing but a single 'hosanna.' But nothing but hosanna isn't enough for life—the hosanna has to be tested in the crucible of doubt, and so on, in that same vein. But I don't meddle in that, I didn't invent it, I'm not answerable for it. Well, they picked their scapegoat, they made me write the criticism column, and so life became possible. We understand that comedy perfectly; I, for instance, simply ask to be annihilated. No, live, they tell me, because there'd be nothing without you. If everything in the universe were sensible, nothing would ever happen. There'd be no events without me, and there have to be events. So against my own grain, I serve to produce events, and do what's irrational, because I'm commanded to. For all their unquestionable intelligence, men take this farce as something serious, and that's their tragedy. They suffer for it, of course... but then again, they live, they live a real life, not a fantastical one, because suffering is life. Without suffering, what pleasure would there be in it? It would turn into one endless church service; it would be holy, but tedious. But what about me? I suffer, and yet I don't live. I'm x in an indeterminate equation. I'm a kind of phantom in life who's lost all beginning and end, and has even forgotten his own name. You're laughing—no, you're not laughing, you're angry again. You're forever angry, all you care about is intelligence, but I'll say it again: I'd give up all this super-stellar existence, all the ranks and honors, just to be transformed into the soul of a merchant's wife weighing eighteen stone, and light candles at God's shrine."
"So even you don't believe in God?" Ivan said, with a smile full of hatred.
"What can I say?—that is, if you're serious—"
"Is there a God, or isn't there?" Ivan cried, with the same savage intensity.
"Ah, so you're serious! My dear fellow, upon my word, I don't know. There! I've said it now!"
"You don't know, but you can see God? No, you're not something apart—you're myself, you're me and nothing more! You're rubbish, you're my fancy!"

"Well, if you like, I hold the same philosophy you do—that much is true. Je pense, donc je suis, that much I know for a fact; everything else, all these worlds, God, even Satan—none of it's proven, to my mind. Does all of that exist on its own, or is it only an emanation of myself, a logical development of my ego, which alone has existed forever? But I'll hurry and stop there, because I believe you're about to jump up and hit me."
"You'd better tell me some story!" Ivan said, wretchedly.

"There's a story on exactly our subject—or rather a legend, not a story. You reproach me with unbelief, you see—you say, but you yourself don't believe. But, my dear fellow, I'm not the only one that way. We're all in quite a muddle over there now, thanks entirely to your science. There used to be atoms, five senses, four elements, and everything hung together somehow. There were even atoms in the ancient world, but since we learned you'd discovered the chemical molecule, and protoplasm, and the devil knows what else, we've had to lower our crest. It's a real mess now—and above all, superstition, scandal; there's just as much scandal among us as among you, you know, a bit more, in fact, and spying too, since we have our own secret police department that takes in private tips. Well, this wild legend belongs to our middle ages—not yours, ours—and no one even among us believes it anymore, except the old ladies weighing eighteen stone, not your old ladies, ours. We have everything you have, I'm letting you in on one of our secrets, out of friendship, though it's forbidden. This legend's about Paradise. There was, they say, here on earth, a thinker and philosopher. He rejected everything—'laws, conscience, faith'—and above all, the afterlife. He died; he expected to go straight into darkness and death, and instead found an afterlife waiting for him. He was astonished and outraged. 'This goes against my principles!' he said. And he was punished for it... that is, forgive me, I'm just repeating what I heard myself, it's only a legend... he was sentenced to walk a quadrillion kilometers in the dark (we've adopted the metric system, you know), and once he's finished that quadrillion, the gates of heaven will open to him and he'll be forgiven—"
"And what torments do you have over there, besides the quadrillion kilometers?" Ivan asked, with a strange eagerness.

"What torments? Ah, don't ask. In the old days we had every kind, but now they've mostly switched to moral punishments—'the stings of conscience' and all that nonsense. We got that from you too, from the general softening of your manners. And who's better off for it? Only those with no conscience at all, because how can conscience torment someone who hasn't got one? But decent people, with conscience and a sense of honor, suffer for it. Reforms, when the ground hasn't been prepared for them, especially institutions copied wholesale from abroad, do nothing but harm! The old-fashioned fire was better. Well, this man, sentenced to the quadrillion kilometers, stood still, looked around, and lay down across the road. 'I won't go, I refuse on principle!' Take the soul of an enlightened Russian atheist and mix it with the soul of the prophet Jonah, who sulked for three days and nights in the belly of the whale, and you get the character of that thinker lying across the road."
"What did he lie down on, out there?"
"Well, I suppose there was something to lie on. You're not laughing?"
"Bravo!" Ivan cried, still with that same strange eagerness. Now he was listening with unexpected curiosity. "So, is he still lying there now?"
"That's exactly the point—he isn't. He lay there nearly a thousand years, and then he got up and went on."

"What an ass!" Ivan cried, laughing nervously, still seeming to be turning something over intently in his mind. "Does it make any difference whether he lies there forever or walks the quadrillion kilometers? It would take a billion years to walk it!"
"Much more than that. I don't have a pencil and paper on me, or I could work it out precisely. But he got there long ago, and that's where the story really begins."
"What, he got there? But how did he manage the billion years to do it?"

"Ah, you keep thinking of our present earth! But our present earth may have repeated itself a billion times already. It's gone extinct, been frozen, cracked, shattered into fragments, broken down into its elements, and turned back into 'the water above the firmament,' then a comet again, a sun again, and from the sun it becomes earth once more—and that same sequence may have repeated endlessly, exactly the same down to the last detail, most unseemly and unbearably tedious—"
"Well, well, what happened once he arrived?"

"Why, the very moment the gates of Paradise opened and he walked in, before he'd even been there two seconds by his watch (though to my mind his watch must have long since dissolved into its elements on the way), he cried out that those two seconds alone were worth walking not just a quadrillion kilometers, but a quadrillion quadrillions, raised to the quadrillionth power! In fact, he sang hosanna, and overdid it so thoroughly that some of the more high-minded people there wouldn't shake his hand at first—he'd turned reactionary far too fast, they said. The Russian temperament. I repeat, it's only a legend. Take it for what it's worth. So that's the sort of thinking we still have about such things, even now."

"I've caught you!" Ivan cried, with an almost childish delight, as though he'd finally managed to remember something. "That story about the quadrillion years—I made it up myself! I was seventeen at the time, at the high school. I invented that anecdote and told it to a schoolmate of mine, Korovkin—this was in Moscow.... The story's so distinctive I couldn't have picked it up anywhere else. I thought I'd forgotten it... but I've recalled it without meaning to—I remembered it myself—you didn't tell it to me! A thousand things get remembered like that without a person meaning to, even in men being led to execution... it's come back to me in a dream. You are that dream! You're a dream, not a living creature!"
"From the sheer force with which you deny I exist," the gentleman laughed, "I'm convinced that you believe in me."
"Not in the slightest! I haven't a hundredth of a grain of faith in you!"
"But you do have a thousandth of a grain. Homeopathic doses might be the strongest, after all. Admit it—you've got faith down to the ten-thousandth of a grain."
"Not for a single minute," Ivan cried, furiously. "But I'd like to believe in you," he added, strangely.

"Aha! There's a confession! But I'm good-natured. I'll come to your aid again. Listen, it was I who caught you, not you me. I told you your own forgotten anecdote on purpose, precisely to destroy your faith in me altogether."
"You're lying. The whole point of your visit is to convince me you exist!"

"Just so. But hesitation, suspense, the conflict between belief and disbelief, is sometimes such torture to a conscientious man like yourself that it's better to just go hang oneself. Knowing you're inclined to believe in me, I administered a dose of disbelief by telling you that anecdote. I lead you toward belief and disbelief by turns, and I have my reasons for it. It's the new method. The moment you disbelieve in me completely, you'll turn right around and start insisting to my face that I'm not a dream but a reality. I know you. Then I'll have achieved my goal, which is an honorable one. I'll plant in you only the tiniest grain of faith, and it'll grow into an oak tree—and such an oak tree that, sitting up in it, you'll long to join the ranks of the 'hermits of the wilderness and the holy women,' because that's exactly what you're secretly longing for. You'll dine on locusts, you'll wander off into the wilderness to save your soul!"
"So it's for the salvation of my soul you're working, is it, you scoundrel?"
"One has to do a good deed now and then. How sour-tempered you are!"
"Fool! Did you ever tempt those holy men who ate locusts and prayed seventeen years in the wilderness until they were overgrown with moss?"

"My dear fellow, I've done nothing else my whole existence. One forgets the entire world, and every other world besides, and clings to a single such saint, because he's a very precious diamond. One soul like that, you know, is sometimes worth a whole constellation. We keep our own system of accounting, you understand. The conquest is priceless! And some of them, I promise you, aren't inferior to you in learning, though you won't believe it. They can contemplate such depths of belief and disbelief at the very same instant that sometimes it really does look as if they're a hair's breadth from being 'turned upside down,' as the actor Gorbunov puts it."
"Well, and did you get your nose pulled?"

"My dear fellow," the visitor observed, sententiously, "it's better to get off with your nose pulled than to have no nose at all. As an afflicted marquis once observed, not long ago (he must have been under a specialist's care), confessing to his spiritual father—a Jesuit. I was there myself, it was simply charming. 'Give me back my nose!' he said, beating his breast. 'My son,' the priest said, evasively, 'all things happen according to the inscrutable decrees of Providence, and what looks like misfortune sometimes leads to extraordinary, if unseen, benefits. If stern fate has robbed you of your nose, it works to your advantage that no one can ever pull you by it again.' 'Holy father, that's no comfort,' the despairing marquis cried. 'I'd be delighted to have my nose pulled every single day of my life, if only it were still in its proper place.' 'My son,' the priest sighed, 'you can't expect every blessing all at once. That's grumbling against Providence, which hasn't forgotten you even in this—because if you complain, as you just did, declaring you'd be glad to have your nose pulled for the rest of your life, your wish has already been granted, indirectly, since in losing your nose, you were led by the nose.'"
"Fool, how stupid!" Ivan cried.

"My dear friend, I only meant to amuse you. But I swear that's genuine Jesuit casuistry, and I swear it happened word for word exactly as I've told it. It happened recently, and gave me a great deal of trouble. The unhappy young man shot himself that very night, once he got home. I stayed by his side right to the very end. Those Jesuit confessionals really are my most delightful entertainment in melancholy moments. Here's another incident, from just the other day. A little blonde Norman girl of twenty—a buxom, guileless beauty that would make your mouth water—comes to an old priest. She bends down and whispers her sin through the grating. 'Why, my daughter, have you fallen again already?' the priest cries. 'O Sancta Maria, what am I hearing! Not the same man this time—how long is this going to go on? Aren't you ashamed?' 'Ah, mon père,' the sinner answers, with tears of repentance, 'ça lui fait tant de plaisir, et à moi si peu de peine!' Imagine, such an answer! I stepped back. It was the cry of nature, better than innocence itself, if you like. I absolved her sin right there and turned to leave, but was forced to turn back. I heard the priest, through the grating, arranging a meeting with her for that evening—though he was an old man, hard as flint, he fell in an instant! It was nature, the truth of nature asserting its rights! What, turning your nose up again? Angry again? I don't know how to please you—"

"Leave me alone, you're beating on my brain like some haunting nightmare," Ivan moaned, wretchedly, helpless before his own apparition. "I'm bored of you, agonizingly, unbearably bored. I'd give anything to shake you off!"

"I'll say it again, moderate your expectations, don't demand 'everything grand and noble' from me, and you'll see how well we get along," the gentleman said, impressively. "You're really angry with me for not appearing to you in a red glow, with thunder and lightning, with scorched wings, but showing myself instead in such a modest shape. You're wounded, first, in your aesthetic feelings, and second, in your pride. How could such a vulgar devil pay a visit to such a great man as yourself! Yes, there's that romantic streak in you, the one Byelinsky mocked so mercilessly. I can't help it, young man—as I was getting ready to come to you, I did think, as a joke, of appearing in the form of a retired general who'd served in the Caucasus, with the star of the Lion and the Sun on my coat. But I was genuinely afraid to do it, because you'd have thrashed me for daring to pin the Lion and the Sun on my coat, instead of at least the Polar Star, or Sirius. And you keep calling me stupid, but mercy on us, I make no claim to be your equal in intelligence. Mephistopheles told Faust he desired evil, but did only good. Well, he can say what he likes—it's quite the opposite with me. I may be the one being in all of creation who loves the truth and genuinely wants good. I was there when the Word, who died on the Cross, rose up into heaven bearing on his breast the soul of the penitent thief. I heard the joyous shrieks of the cherubim, singing and shouting hosanna, and the thunderous rapture of the seraphim that shook heaven and all creation, and I swear to you, by everything sacred, I longed to join the choir and shout hosanna with all of them. The word had all but escaped me, had nearly broken from my lips... you know how susceptible and aesthetically impressionable I am. But common sense—oh, a most unfortunate trait in my character—kept me within proper bounds, and I let the moment pass! Because what would have happened, I thought to myself, what would have happened after my hosanna? Everything on earth would have been snuffed out at once, and no events could have occurred at all. And so, purely out of a sense of duty, and my social position, I was forced to suppress that good moment, and stick to my nasty task. Somebody else takes all the credit for everything good, and nothing but nastiness is left for me. But I don't envy him the honor of a life of idle fraud—I'm not ambitious. Why am I, of all beings in the world, condemned to be cursed by every decent person, even kicked around, since taking on mortal form means I sometimes have to bear those consequences? I know, of course, there's a secret behind it, but they won't tell me the secret for anything, because if I understood its meaning, I might just bellow out hosanna, and the indispensable minus would vanish at once, and good sense would reign supreme over the whole world. And that, of course, would mean the end of everything—even of magazines and newspapers, since who would subscribe to them then? I know that in the end I'll be reconciled. I too will walk my quadrillion and learn the secret. But until that happens, I sulk and carry out my destiny, even against the grain—which is, to ruin thousands in order to save one. How many souls have had to be ruined, how many honorable reputations destroyed, for the sake of that one righteous man, Job, over whom they made such a fool of me in the old days! Yes, until the secret's revealed, there are two kinds of truth for me—theirs, over there, which I know nothing about so far, and my own. And there's no telling which will turn out to be the better one.... Are you asleep?"
"I might as well be," Ivan groaned, angrily. "All my stupid ideas—outgrown, thrashed out long ago, and tossed aside like a dead carcass—you're serving them back to me as something new!"
"There's just no pleasing you! And here I thought I'd win you over with my literary style. That hosanna in the heavens wasn't bad, was it? And then that ironic tone à la Heine, eh?"
"No, I was never such a lackey! Then how could my own soul have spawned a lackey like you?"

"My dear fellow, I know a most charming, appealing young Russian gentleman, a young thinker and a great lover of literature and art, author of a promising poem titled The Grand Inquisitor. I was only thinking of him!"
"I forbid you to speak of The Grand Inquisitor," Ivan cried, crimson with shame.
"And the Geological Cataclysm. Remember that? Now that was a poem!"
"Hold your tongue, or I'll kill you!"

"You'll kill me? No, excuse me, I'm going to speak. I came here to treat myself to that very pleasure. Oh, I love the dreams of my eager young friends, quivering with hunger for life! 'There are new men,' you decided last spring, right before you set off to come here, 'they propose to tear down everything and start with cannibalism. Foolish fellows—they never asked my advice! I maintain that nothing needs to be torn down, that all we need is to destroy the idea of God in man, that's where the real work begins. That's what we must start with. Oh, blind race, with no understanding! The moment every last man has denied God—and I believe that period, comparable to a geological age, will come to pass—the old conception of the universe will collapse on its own, without any cannibalism, and, what's more, so will the old morality, and everything will begin anew. Men will unite to wring from life everything it can offer, but only for joy and happiness in this present world. Man will be lifted up on a spirit of divine, Titanic pride, and the man-god will appear. Hour by hour, extending his conquest of nature infinitely through will and science, man will feel such lofty joy, hour by hour, in the doing of it, that it will make up for all his old dreams of heavenly joys. Everyone will know he is mortal, and will accept death proudly and calmly, like a god. His pride will teach him it's pointless to grieve that life is only a moment, and he'll love his brother with no need of reward. Love will be enough only for a moment of life, but the very awareness of its brevity will only intensify its fire, fire that today is squandered on dreams of eternal love beyond the grave'—and so on, and so on, in the same vein. Charming!"
Ivan sat with his eyes fixed on the floor, hands pressed to his ears, but he began trembling all over. The voice went on.

"The question now, my young thinker reflected, is whether such a period could ever really come. If it does, everything is settled, and humanity is fixed forever. But since, given man's ingrained stupidity, this can't come about for at least a thousand years, anyone who recognizes the truth even now may fairly order his own life however he pleases, on these new principles. In that sense, 'everything is permitted' for him. What's more, even if this age never arrives at all, since there's no God anyway, and no immortality, the new man may as well become the man-god, even if he's the only one of his kind in the entire world, and, elevated to his new rank, he may cheerfully step over every barrier of the old slave-man's morality, if it comes to that. There's no law for God. Where God stands, that ground is holy. Wherever I stand will become, at once, the foremost place... 'everything is permitted,' and that's the end of it! All very charming; but if you want to swindle someone, why do you need a moral sanction to do it? But that's our modern Russian, through and through. He simply can't bring himself to swindle without a moral sanction for it. He's so terribly in love with the truth—"

The visitor talked on, clearly carried away by his own eloquence, his voice rising louder and louder, watching his host with an ironic eye. But he never got to finish; Ivan suddenly snatched a glass off the table and hurled it at him.

"Ah, mais c'est bête enfin," the man cried, jumping up off the sofa and shaking tea drops off himself. "He remembers Luther's inkstand! He takes me for a dream and throws glasses at a dream! Just like a woman! I suspected you were only pretending to stop up your ears."
A loud, persistent knocking suddenly sounded at the window. Ivan jumped up from the sofa.
"Do you hear? You'd better open it," the visitor cried. "It's your brother Alyosha, with the most interesting and surprising news, I'll bet you anything!"
"Quiet, deceiver, I knew it was Alyosha, I could feel him coming, and of course he hasn't come for nothing—of course he's bringing 'news,'" Ivan exclaimed, frantically.
"Open up, open up for him. There's a snowstorm out there, and he's your brother. Monsieur sait-il le temps qu'il fait? C'est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors."

The knocking went on. Ivan wanted to rush to the window, but something seemed to have chained his arms and legs. He strained with all his might to break free, but in vain. The knocking at the window grew louder and louder. At last the chains broke, and Ivan leapt up off the sofa. He looked around wildly. Both candles had nearly burned out; the glass he'd just thrown at his visitor stood on the table before him, and there was no one on the sofa across the room. The knocking on the window frame continued, insistently, but it was nowhere near as loud as it had seemed in his dream; on the contrary, it was quite muted.
"It wasn't a dream! No, I swear it wasn't a dream, it all just happened!" Ivan cried. He rushed to the window and threw open the sash.
"Alyosha, I told you not to come," he shouted fiercely at his brother. "In two words—what do you want? In two words, do you hear?"
"An hour ago Smerdyakov hanged himself," Alyosha answered, from the yard.
"Come round to the steps, I'll open the door at once," said Ivan, going to let Alyosha in.
